question: Who shifted the capital of Magadha from Pataliputra to Vaishali?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shishunaga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shishunaga, founder of the Shishunaga (Saisunaga) dynasty, shifted the capital from Pataliputra to Vaishali (शिशुनाग — राजधानी वैशाली)

 

• His successor was Kakavarman, also called Kalasoka.

 

• The dynasty followed the Haryankas and preceded the Nandas.

 

• Vaishali was formerly the Licchavi/Vajji capital.

 

• Vaishali was earlier the Licchavi and Vajji capital, which was annexed by Ajatashatru. Shishunaga used it as a new base for Magadha, and the capital later went back to Pataliputra.

 

• The notes name Shishunaga as the founder-ruler of this dynasty, with Kalasoka as his successor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalasoka was the son of Shishunaga.

 

• Shishunaga is said to have destroyed the Pradyota dynasty of Avanti.

 

• Pataliputra was Udayin's foundation.

 

• The Shishunaga dynasty followed the Haryankas and preceded the Nandas.

 

• Vaishali also hosted the Second Buddhist Council. After the Shishunagas, the capital was Pataliputra again under the Nandas, so Vaishali was only a temporary seat.

 

NOTE

 

• Bimbisara (Option 1): Bimbisara ruled from Rajagriha and lived before Pataliputra became a capital. He neither founded nor shifted any capital to Vaishali.

 

• Kalasoka (Option 3): Kalasoka was the son and successor of Shishunaga. The shift to Vaishali is credited to Shishunaga, so Kalasoka is not the answer.

 

• Dhananda (Option 4): Dhananda ended the Nanda line and came after the Shishunagas. By then the capital had returned to Pataliputra, so he did not move it to Vaishali.

question: The Second Buddhist Council was held at Vaishali in 383 BC during the reign of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kalasoka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Second Buddhist Council was held at Vaishali in 383 BC during the reign of Kalasoka (Kakavarman), son of Shishunaga (द्वितीय बौद्ध संगीति — वैशाली, कालाशोक)

 

• Kalasoka was a ruler of the Shishunaga dynasty.

 

• The First Council was held earlier in Ajatashatru's reign.

 

• The dynasty's capital was Vaishali, which hosted the council.

 

• The Second Council was called to settle differences on monastic rules, and this dispute later led to the Buddhist sects. Vaishali was the venue.

 

• Count the councils: Rajgir (First), Vaishali (Second), Pataliputra (Third, Ashoka), Kashmir (Fourth, Kanishka).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Third Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka.

 

• The Fourth Council was held under Kanishka.

 

• The Second Council dealt with disputes over monastic rules.

 

• The Buddhist sects Sthaviravada and Mahasanghika emerged from this period of disputes.

 

• Kalasoka's father was Shishunaga. Remember 383 BC and Vaishali together, because the year is given in the notes and is a favourite for one-line questions.

 

NOTE

 

• Ajatashatru (Option 2): Ajatashatru presided over the First Council, held at Rajgir. The Second Council came about a century later at Vaishali, so he is not the answer.

 

• Bimbisara (Option 3): Bimbisara belonged to the earliest Haryanka period and was a contemporary of the Buddha. He lived long before the Second Council.

 

• Mahapadma Nanda (Option 4): Mahapadma Nanda belonged to the Nanda dynasty in the 4th century BC. The Second Council took place in 383 BC under the Shishunaga king Kalasoka.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Shishunaga dynasty:

1. Shishunaga shifted the capital to Vaishali.

2. Kalasoka was the son of Shishunaga.

3. The First Buddhist Council was held in the reign of Kalasoka.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The capital shift and the Kalasoka-Shishunaga relationship are accurate; the claim about the First Council is the error. Shishunaga moved the capital to Vaishali, and Kalasoka (Kakavarman) was his son; the Second (not First) Council was in Kalasoka's reign (शिशुनाग — वैशाली; कालाशोक — द्वितीय संगीति)

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: the First Council was in Ajatashatru's reign.

 

• The Second Council was held at Vaishali in 383 BC.

 

• The Shishunagas were succeeded by the Nandas.

 

• Question writers often swap First and Second Councils; know the kings: Ajatashatru (First) and Kalasoka (Second). The Shishunagas were a short dynasty.

 

• Shishunaga reportedly destroyed Avanti's power, per tradition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Order: Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda.

 

• Kalasoka's other name is Kakavarman.

 

• Vaishali was the venue of the Second Council.

 

• The Nandas succeeded the Shishunagas.

 

• Kalasoka was also known as Kakavarman. The Shishunaga rule was short compared with the Haryankas and Nandas, and in the notes Kalasoka is the last named ruler. The Shishunaga dynasty also ties to Avanti, since tradition says Shishunaga weakened the power of Pradyota's line.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 3 is wrong, so options that count it as correct, such as 2 and 3, cannot be right. The First Council took place in Ajatashatru's reign, not Kalasoka's.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Statement 1 is correct but Statement 3 is false, so the combination 1 and 3 fails. The Council under Kalasoka was the Second one.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): All three cannot hold because the First Council was under the Haryanka king Ajatashatru. Only the first two statements are correct.

question: Which ruler was the founder of the Nanda Dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mahapadma Nanda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahapadma Nanda was the founder of the Nanda dynasty and a powerful ruler of it; he is regarded as the first historical ruler to build a vast empire in north India (महापद्म नंद — नंद वंश के संस्थापक)

 

• The Nandas were India's first empire builders, with nine rulers in all.

 

• Mahapadma added Kalinga to the Magadhan empire.

 

• The last Nanda ruler was Dhananda.

 

• The Nandas have a special place as the first empire builders, and they had nine rulers. Mahapadma Nanda's extensive conquests include Kalinga.

 

• The question has appeared as a CHSL PYQ and is repeated often.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Nanda dynasty succeeded the Shishunagas.

 

• The Nandas were overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya with Kautilya's help.

 

• The Nandas ruled in the 4th century BC.

 

• The dynasty followed the Shishunagas.

 

• They were overthrown with Kautilya's help. Mahapadma Nanda is described in the Puranas as the destroyer of the Kshatriyas, which is why he is called a great conqueror.

 

NOTE

 

• Ashoka (Option 1): Ashoka was a Mauryan emperor, which came after the Nandas. He cannot be the founder of the Nanda dynasty. Ashoka belongs to the later Mauryan line altogether.

 

• Dhananda (Option 3): Dhananda, the final Nanda king, was overthrown by Chandragupta. He was not the founder of the dynasty, as that was Mahapadma Nanda.

 

• Chandragupta Maurya (Option 4): Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nandas and founded the Mauryan dynasty. He is the founder of a different dynasty, not of the Nandas.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Nanda dynasty:

1. The Nandas are described as India's first empire builders.

2. There were nine rulers in the dynasty.

3. Dhananda was the first ruler of the dynasty.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The empire-builder tag and the count of nine rulers are accurate; calling Dhananda the first ruler is the mistake. The Nandas were India's first empire builders, and there were nine rulers in all; Mahapadma Nanda was the powerful early ruler and Dhananda the last ruler (नंद वंश — नौ शासक, अंतिम धनानंद)

 

• Statement 3 is false: Dhananda was the last ruler.

 

• Their empire stretched widely, including Kalinga.

 

• They were overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya with Kautilya's help.

 

• The Nandas were the first empire builders because they united much of north India under Magadha. Their wealth and army were big enough that Alexander's soldiers reportedly refused to march further east.

 

• Nanda tax collection became oppressive, which led to their downfall.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nanda rule is followed by Maurya rule.

 

• Mahapadma Nanda is credited with founding the dynasty.

 

• The Nandas were rich in wealth and military strength.

 

• The Nandas were of low social origin per Puranic tradition.

 

• The next dynasty was the Mauryan dynasty. The count of nine rulers is often asked, along with the name of the last king Dhananda.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 3 is wrong because Dhananda came at the very end of the dynasty, not the start. Hence the combination 2 and 3 fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Statement 1 is correct, but Statement 3 is false, as the dynasty began with Mahapadma Nanda. So 1 and 3 together cannot be right.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Since Statement 3 is false, all three cannot be correct. Only the statements on empire builders and the nine rulers are true.

question: The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela records that which dynasty had conquered Kalinga before Ashoka?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nandas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela of Kalinga records that the Nandas had conquered Kalinga, i.e. Mahapadma Nanda took Kalinga before Ashoka (हाथीगुम्फा अभिलेख — नंदों द्वारा कलिंग विजय)

 

• Kalinga was added to the Magadhan empire by Mahapadma Nanda.

 

• Ashoka's own conquest of Kalinga took place later, in the Kalinga War of the Mauryan period.

 

• Kharavela was the king of Kalinga.

 

• The inscription is the main source for Kalinga's earlier link with the Nandas. It proves that the Nandas conquered Kalinga before Ashoka's war.

 

• The inscription also tells of Kharavela's own achievements.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Hathigumpha inscription is at Udayagiri hills near Bhubaneswar.

 

• It is in Brahmi script and Prakrit language.

 

• Kharavela belonged to the Mahameghavahana dynasty.

 

• Hathigumpha is near Bhubaneswar in Odisha.

 

• Ashoka's Kalinga War led him to adopt Dhamma. Do not mix Kharavela with Ashoka, because the Hathigumpha record is the work of the Kalinga king, not a Mauryan edict.

 

NOTE

 

• Haryankas (Option 1): The Haryankas under Bimbisara conquered Anga, but the Hathigumpha inscription does not credit them with conquering Kalinga. It refers to the Nandas.

 

• Shishunagas (Option 3): The Shishunagas are not associated with Kalinga in the inscription. They are remembered for Vaishali and the Second Council. The record points to the Nandas alone.

 

• Mauryas (Option 4): The Mauryas conquered Kalinga after the Nandas, under Ashoka, in the famous Kalinga War. The inscription says the Nandas took it earlier. The inscription does not link them to Kalinga.

question: Who was the last ruler of the Nanda dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dhananda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The last king of the Nanda dynasty was Dhana Nanda, whose harsh tax collection made him unpopular; Chandragupta Maurya overthrew him (धनानंद — अंतिम नंद शासक)

 

• Chandragupta Maurya and Kautilya used the people's anger to launch a popular movement against Nanda rule.

 

• His reign coincided with Alexander's invasion of the north-west of India.

 

• After his fall the Maurya dynasty began.

 

• Chandragupta, advised by Kautilya, captured Pataliputra, and the Nanda reign thus gave way to the Mauryan dynasty.

 

• The last Nanda king is also known as Dhana Nanda.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tradition credits the last Nanda king with a very large army and great wealth.

 

• Chandragupta established the Maurya Empire around 321 BC.

 

• Kautilya is also known as Chanakya.

 

• The Mudrarakshasa play of Vishakhadatta deals with the fall of the Nandas.

 

• Chandragupta's rise is dated about 321 BC. After Dhananda's fall the Mauryan capital remained at Pataliputra, which was the Nanda capital as well.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahapadma Nanda (Option 2): Mahapadma Nanda was the founder and a powerful ruler of the dynasty. He ruled early in the dynasty and was not the last.

 

• Kaivarta (Option 3): Kaivarta is not the last Nanda ruler; that was Dhananda. Traditional lists give other names for the intermediate kings. The name of the real last ruler is what you must remember.

 

• Panduka Nanda (Option 4): Panduka Nanda is one of the earlier Nanda kings in traditional lists. The last ruler, whom Chandragupta overthrew, was Dhananda.

question: What was the main reason for the popular anger against the last Nanda ruler Dhananda?
option_2: The harsh way he collected taxes
option_3: His shifting of the capital to Vaishali
solution_text:
The correct answer is The harsh way he collected taxes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• People deeply resented the harsh way Dhananda collected taxes; Chandragupta Maurya and Kautilya used this anger to launch a popular movement against Nanda rule (कठोर कर वसूली — धनानंद का विरोध)

 

• This discontent helped Chandragupta overthrow the Nandas and found the Mauryan Empire.

 

• Kautilya (Chanakya) was the strategist behind the movement.

 

• The episode occurred around the time of Alexander's invasion.

 

• Taxation was an important cause of unrest, and Chandragupta along with Kautilya turned this unrest into a popular movement. This ended the Nanda dynasty.

 

• Administration and revenue are major themes in questions of the period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chandragupta Maurya came to the throne around 321 BC.

 

• The Mudrarakshasa play of Vishakhadatta dramatises the fall of the Nandas.

 

• Kautilya authored the Arthashastra.

 

• Kautilya is also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta.

 

• The Nandas were succeeded by the Mauryas. Remember the sequence: harsh taxation, popular anger, a movement led by Chandragupta and Kautilya, and the fall of the Nandas.

 

NOTE

 

• His conversion to Jainism (Option 1): Conversion to Jainism is linked in the notes to Udayin, not Dhananda. It is therefore not the reason for the popular anger.

 

• His shifting of the capital to Vaishali (Option 3): Shishunaga, not Dhananda, shifted the capital to Vaishali. Shifting a capital was not the cause of the movement against the Nandas.

 

• His defeat by Ajatashatru (Option 4): Ajatashatru lived centuries before Dhananda and belonged to the Haryanka dynasty. Dhananda's rule was not ended by such a defeat.

question: Alexander invaded India during the period of which dynasty of Magadha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nanda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alexander's invasion of India took place during the period of the Nanda dynasty, whose last ruler was Dhananda (सिकंदर का आक्रमण — नंद वंश के समय)

 

• Alexander invaded the north-west, the former region of Gandhara (Taxila).

 

• Soon after, Chandragupta Maurya replaced the Nandas.

 

• The Nandas were a powerful empire in the east at that time.

 

• Alexander's army reached the Beas river and refused to march to the Nanda kingdom in the east. Soon after, Chandragupta Maurya rose to power.

 

• Remember the order of this period: Nandas, Alexander, Mauryas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Greek invasion is dated 326 BC.

 

• Chandragupta Maurya later defeated the Greek satraps left by Alexander.

 

• Seleucus Nikator was Alexander's general.

 

• Alexander came to India in 326 BC.

 

• Chandragupta later defeated Seleucus Nikator. The Greek writers called the Nanda kingdom Prasii (Prachyas) and described its huge army of foot soldiers, horses, chariots and elephants.

 

NOTE

 

• Haryanka (Option 1): The Haryankas ruled in the 6th-5th centuries BC, long before Alexander. Alexander's invasion came in the 4th century BC. Alexander's date is far later than this dynasty.

 

• Shishunaga (Option 2): The Shishunagas also ruled before the Nandas, around the 5th century BC. They were no longer in power when Alexander invaded.

 

• Maurya (Option 4): The Mauryas began only after Alexander's invasion, when Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas. The invasion took place in the Nanda period.

question: Which ancient Sanskrit grammarian lived during the time of the Nandas?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Panini.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Panini, the great Sanskrit grammarian, lived during the time of the Nandas and composed the Ashtadhyayi (पाणिनि — नंद काल, अष्टाध्यायी)

 

• The Ashtadhyayi is the earliest known and most comprehensive work on Sanskrit grammar.

 

• It means 'Eight Chapters' and contains about 4000 sutras.

 

• His work laid the foundation for classical Sanskrit.

 

• Panini's Ashtadhyayi is the earliest and most comprehensive work on Sanskrit grammar. It is the basis for classical Sanskrit and is repeatedly asked in SSC exams.

 

• Panini lived during the Nanda period, as stated in the notes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Patanjali wrote the Mahabhashya, a commentary on Panini, in the Shunga period.

 

• Kalidasa was a Gupta-age poet.

 

• Aryabhata was a Gupta-age mathematician-astronomer.

 

• Panini is from the north-west of India.

 

• Patanjali also wrote the Yoga Sutras per tradition. Panini's Ashtadhyayi gave rules for Sanskrit as spoken in his time and is still treated as the standard text for the language.

 

NOTE

 

• Kalidasa (Option 2): Kalidasa was a poet of the Gupta age, many centuries after the Nandas. He wrote Sanskrit literary works rather than a work on grammar.

 

• Aryabhata (Option 3): Aryabhata was a Gupta-period astronomer and mathematician. He lived centuries after the Nandas and is known for the Aryabhatiya. He is known for science, not grammar.

 

• Patanjali (Option 4): Patanjali wrote the Mahabhashya, a commentary on Panini, in the Shunga period. He lived after the Nandas, so he is not the grammarian of that time.

question: The Ashtadhyayi of Panini contains approximately how many sutras?
solution_text:
The correct answer is About 4000.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ashtadhyayi ('Eight Chapters') contains approximately 3959 to 4000 sutras (rules), making it the earliest known and most comprehensive work on Sanskrit grammar (अष्टाध्यायी — लगभग 4000 सूत्र)

 

• It was composed by Panini, who lived during the time of the Nandas.

 

• Its name reflects its eight chapters.

 

• It remains the base of classical Sanskrit grammar.

 

• Panini's sutras are short and precise formulas, which makes the work compact. Its eight chapters give the name Ashtadhyayi.

 

• Both the number and the name are asked in exams.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Panini was from Shalatura in north-west India (Gandhara region).

 

• Patanjali's Mahabhashya comments on it.

 

• Sanskrit is an Indo-Aryan language.

 

• The Ashtadhyayi was written during the Nanda period.

 

• Panini's grammar is the foundation of classical Sanskrit. The Ashtadhyayi uses very short sutras and is arranged in eight chapters, each divided into four sections (padas).

 

NOTE

 

• 692 (Option 1): 692 is far less than the approximate 4000 sutras in the Ashtadhyayi. The work is the biggest grammar work of its time. The number is wildly off the mark, as the book is much bigger.

 

• 1632 (Option 2): 1632 is not the figure given for Panini's work. The Ashtadhyayi contains close to 4000 sutras in eight chapters. That number has no basis in the standard accounts.

 

• 7012 (Option 4): 7012 is nearly double the real number. The Ashtadhyayi has roughly 3959 to 4000 sutras. That number is not what the text contains.

question:
Match the rulers with their kingdoms/dynasties:

(a) Prasenajit  (i) Avanti

(b) Pradyota  (ii) Kosala

(c) Bimbisara  (iii) Haryanka dynasty

(d) Dhananda  (iv) Nanda dynasty
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Prasenajit ruled Kosala, Pradyota ruled Avanti, Bimbisara founded the Haryanka dynasty and Dhananda was the last Nanda king, so a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (प्रसेनजित-कोसल, प्रद्योत-अवंति, बिंबिसार-हर्यंक, धनानंद-नंद)

 

• Prasenajit's capital was Sravasti; Pradyota's was Ujjain.

 

• Bimbisara's capital was Rajagriha.

 

• The ruler of the Nanda dynasty named here fell to Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• Ruler-kingdom pairs are easily tested by swapping neighbouring states. Memorise Prasenajit-Kosala, Pradyota-Avanti, Bimbisara-Magadha.

 

• The Haryankas ruled Magadha and the Nandas succeeded them after the Shishunagas. Each pair in the correct answer ties a ruler with his realm, so memorise them as ruler-realm units. Prasenajit ruled Kosala from Sravasti, and Pradyota ruled Avanti from Ujjain. Bimbisara founded the Haryanka line in Magadha, and Dhananda was the last of the nine Nandas. Revise the pairs as units and check them against neighbouring states to avoid swaps.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kosala, Avanti, Vatsa and Magadha were the four survivors.

 

• Prasenajit was Bimbisara's brother-in-law.

 

• The Nanda king named in the match ruled in the 4th century BC.

 

• Kosala's capital was Sravasti and Avanti's was Ujjain.

 

• The Nanda ruler here was overthrown by Chandragupta. Such ruler-dynasty matches are common in SSC papers.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): Prasenajit-Avanti and Pradyota-Kosala are swapped. Prasenajit ruled Kosala, while Pradyota ruled Avanti. Such a pairing is wrong in both of these cases.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 2): Bimbisara-Nanda and Dhananda-Haryanka are swapped. Bimbisara founded the Haryanka dynasty and Dhananda was the last Nanda king. Both these pairings are therefore wrong.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 3): This set mismatches all four pairs. None of the rulers belongs to the kingdom or dynasty it is paired with. Hence no pair here can be right.

question:
Match the following Mahajanapadas with their capitals:

(1) Vatsa  (a) Rajagriha

(2) Magadha  (b) Kaushambi

(3) Kuru  (c) Ujjayini

(4) Avanti  (d) Indraprastha
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vatsa - Kaushambi, Magadha - Rajagriha, Kuru - Indraprastha and Avanti - Ujjayini (Ujjain) are the correct pairs, giving 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c (वत्स-कौशांबी, मगध-राजगृह, कुरु-इंद्रप्रस्थ, अवंति-उज्जैन)

 

• Magadha's capital was Rajagriha before Pataliputra was founded by Udayin.

 

• Vatsa and Avanti were among the four survivors.

 

• Indraprastha is identified with the area around Delhi.

 

• This is a genuine PYQ in the style of SSC Steno. The same four pairs were asked, so memorise them well.

 

• Ujjayini is another name of Ujjain.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Magadha's capital was also called Girivraja.

 

• Avanti had a second capital at Mahismati.

 

• Vatsa lay on the Yamuna.

 

• Kuru was in the Delhi region.

 

• Avanti was in Malwa. Ujjayini and Ujjain are the same city, and the PYQ used the older name, so be ready for both forms. Always revise Kuru-Indraprastha with Surasena-Mathura as neighbours that examiners like to interchange.

 

NOTE

 

• 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d (Option 2): Vatsa-Rajagriha and Magadha-Kaushambi are swapped. Vatsa's capital was Kaushambi and Magadha's capital was Rajagriha. Both of these pairs are therefore reversed.

 

• 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a (Option 3): Vatsa-Ujjayini and Magadha-Indraprastha are wrong. Ujjayini was the capital of Avanti and Indraprastha was the capital of Kuru. Both of these pairs are therefore wrongly matched.

 

• 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b (Option 4): Vatsa-Indraprastha and Magadha-Ujjayini are wrong. These capitals belong to Kuru and Avanti, respectively. Hence both pairs are wrongly matched. Both pairs are therefore reversed in this set.

question:
Consider the following statements about the sources on the Mahajanapadas:

1. The Anguttara Nikaya lists sixteen great kingdoms.

2. Jain texts also speak of sixteen kingdoms.

3. Fifteen of the sixteen Mahajanapadas lay in the south.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The two source claims (Buddhist and Jain) are accurate, while the south-heavy distribution is reversed. The Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya lists sixteen great kingdoms and Jain texts also speak of sixteen kingdoms; but fifteen lay in the north and only one (Asmaka) in the south (अंगुत्तर निकाय और जैन ग्रंथ — सोलह महाजनपद)

 

• Statement 3 reverses the actual position and is false.

 

• The only southern Mahajanapada, Asmaka, was on the Godavari with capital Potali.

 

• So our two sources are a Buddhist text and Jain texts.

 

• The question tests the numbers: sixteen kingdoms, fifteen in the north and one in the south. The two sources are the Anguttara Nikaya and the Jain texts.

 

• Asmaka was the southern one, on the Godavari.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahajanapada means 'great realm' (Maha + Janapada).

 

• By the mid-6th century BC only four remained.

 

• Magadha was the strongest of them.

 

• Only four of the sixteen survived by the mid-6th century BC.

 

• Magadha eventually became the strongest. Asmaka's capital Potali is also written as Podana, and both forms may appear in options.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 3 is false, as fifteen of the sixteen Mahajanapadas lay in the north, not in the south. Hence 2 and 3 cannot be right.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Statement 3 is false because only Asmaka was in the south. So the combination 1 and 3 is incorrect. The only southern state was Asmaka.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Since Statement 3 is false, the combination of all three cannot be correct. Only statements 1 and 2 are right. This makes the pairing of statements wrong.

question:
Consider the following statements about the four surviving kingdoms of the mid-6th century BC:

1. Vatsa lay along the Yamuna with its capital at Kausambi.

2. Avanti's most important ruler was Pradyota, with capital at Ujjain.

3. Kosala's famous ruler Prasenajit had his capital at Kausambi.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vatsa and Avanti descriptions are accurate, whereas Kosala's capital is misstated. Vatsa lay on the Yamuna with its capital Kausambi, and Avanti had Pradyota as its most important ruler with Ujjain as capital; Statement 3 is wrong because Kosala's capital was Sravasti (वत्स — कौशांबी; अवंति — प्रद्योत; कोसल — श्रावस्ती)

 

• The fourth survivor was Magadha.

 

• Prasenajit, a highly educated king, ruled Kosala.

 

• Kausambi is near modern Allahabad.

 

• Capitals of the four survivors are tested again and again: Kausambi, Ujjain, Sravasti and Rajagriha. Mixing up neighbouring capitals is a typical trap in statement questions, so learn each capital with its ruler.

 

• Pradyota is the Avanti ruler and Prasenajit the Kosala ruler; examiners often swap these two names.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Magadha eventually outlasted the other three.

 

• Bimbisara married Prasenajit's sister.

 

• Avanti was later absorbed by Magadha.

 

• Vatsa lay on the Yamuna near modern Allahabad, while Kosala lay to its north-east in the Gangetic plain around Sravasti.

 

• Avanti had a southern centre at Mahismati on the Narmada besides Ujjain. Among the four survivors, Magadha alone had its capital in Bihar, while the other three lay in Uttar Pradesh and Malwa.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 3 wrongly places Prasenajit's capital at Kausambi. Kosala's capital was Sravasti, so every combination containing Statement 3 is wrong, including the pair of Statements 2 and 3.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Statement 1 is correct about Vatsa, but Statement 3 is false because Kausambi was the capital of Vatsa and not of Kosala. So Statements 1 and 3 cannot be accepted together.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): All three cannot be correct, as Statement 3 confuses the capitals of Kosala and Vatsa. Only the statements about Vatsa on the Yamuna and Avanti under Pradyota are right.

question:
Consider the following statements about Panini:

1. He lived during the time of the Nandas.

2. He composed the Ashtadhyayi.

3. The Ashtadhyayi is a work on Buddhist philosophy.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The period and authorship of Panini are accurate, whereas the subject of his work is misdescribed. Panini lived during the Nanda period and composed the Ashtadhyayi, the earliest known and most comprehensive work on Sanskrit grammar with about 4000 sutras; it is not a work on Buddhist philosophy (पाणिनि — अष्टाध्यायी, संस्कृत व्याकरण)

 

• Ashtadhyayi means 'Eight Chapters'.

 

• So Statement 3 is false.

 

• Panini's work is a milestone in linguistics.

 

• Panini's grammar has about 4000 sutras arranged in eight chapters. It is the earliest and most comprehensive work on Sanskrit grammar known today, and its brevity is legendary.

 

• A common trap is to link Panini with Buddhism or with Mauryan administration, but he was a grammarian of the Nanda period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Patanjali later wrote the Mahabhashya on it.

 

• The Nandas ruled in the 4th century BC.

 

• Panini's grammar fixed classical Sanskrit.

 

• Panini's era is the Nanda period, in the 4th century BC, when Magadha was the leading power.

 

• His rules fixed the standard form of classical Sanskrit and are still studied.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Statement 3 is false because the Ashtadhyayi is a work on Sanskrit grammar, not on Buddhist philosophy. So the pair of Statements 2 and 3 cannot both be correct.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Statement 1 is true but Statement 3 is false, so the pair 1 and 3 fails. The Ashtadhyayi deals with the rules of language and grammar, not with religious philosophy.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three cannot be true, since Statement 3 mislabels the subject of the Ashtadhyayi. Only the first two statements, on the Nanda period and the authorship, hold good.

question:
Assertion (A): Magadha emerged as the most powerful Mahajanapada of north India.

Reason (R): Its soil was fertile, it had war elephants, and iron ores lay in the hills near Rajgir.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Magadha's fertile plains, war elephants, and iron and copper deposits (Rajgir, Gaya), plus the Ganga and Son, explain why it became the most powerful state (मगध का उत्कर्ष — उपजाऊ भूमि, हाथी, लोहा)

 

• These resources gave economic surplus and military strength.

 

• Magadha became the nerve centre of political activity in north India.

 

• Rajagriha was its early capital.

 

• The reasons for Magadha's rise go together: fertile plains, iron, elephants and rivers. Together they made it the nerve centre of political activity in north India.

 

• Magadha then produced three early dynasties in turn: the Haryankas, Shishunagas and Nandas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Magadha is modern Bihar.

 

• The rise of Magadha led to the first empire under the Nandas.

 

• It was later the core of the Mauryan Empire.

 

• Magadha's capitals were Rajagriha first and later Pataliputra.

 

• The Mauryan empire also rose from the same Magadhan base. Questions on Magadha's rise are asked both as assertion-reason and as 'which was NOT a reason'.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): R is a correct explanation of A, as fertile soil, elephants and iron explain Magadha's power. This choice wrongly says the reason is true but not the right explanation.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): R is true, as the notes state Magadha's fertile soil, war elephants and iron ores near Rajgir. This choice wrongly calls the reason false, though it is an accurate statement.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): A is true, since Magadha did become the most powerful Mahajanapada of north India. This choice wrongly calls the assertion false although history confirms it.

question:
Assertion (A): Bimbisara followed a policy of matrimonial alliances.

Reason (R): His marriages with Kosaladevi and Chellana secured peace with Kosala and made his northern frontier safe.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Marriage to Kosaladevi (Kosala) and Chellana (Licchavi of Vaishali) secured peace and a safe northern frontier and brought the Kasi region, which is exactly what his alliance policy aimed at (वैवाहिक संबंध — कोसलदेवी, चेल्लना)

 

• These alliances strengthened Magadha without war.

 

• Bimbisara was a contemporary of Mahavira and Buddha.

 

• He was killed by his son Ajatashatru.

 

• The Kosala marriage gave peace and Kasi, while the Licchavi marriage secured the north. These marriages expanded Magadha's influence without wars.

 

• His peaceful policy was later replaced by Ajatashatru's wars against the Vajjis.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kosala's king Prasenajit was his brother-in-law.

 

• The alliance with Vaishali's Licchavis was later broken by Ajatashatru's war on the Vajjis.

 

• Magadha's growth thereafter was rapid.

 

• Bimbisara ruled c. 546-494 BC per the notes and was killed by his son.

 

• Prasenajit of Kosala was his brother-in-law. Bimbisara's third known marriage, to a Madra princess Khema, is traditional but is not in these notes.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): R is the actual explanation of A, because the marriages were the alliance policy in practice. This choice wrongly says R does not explain A.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): R is true because the marriages did secure peace with Kosala and a safe northern frontier. This choice wrongly says R is false when the notes confirm it.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): A is true, since Bimbisara did follow a policy of matrimonial alliances. This choice wrongly states that A is false, which contradicts the notes.

question:
Assertion (A): The Nandas are regarded as India's first empire builders.

Reason (R): Mahapadma Nanda added Kalinga to the Magadhan empire, as recorded in the Hathigumpha inscription.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Nandas extended Magadhan rule far beyond the Gangetic heartland, and Mahapadma Nanda's conquest of Kalinga, mentioned in Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription, illustrates this wide empire (नंद — प्रथम साम्राज्य निर्माता)

 

• They had nine rulers in all.

 

• Their power was inherited by the Mauryas.

 

• Mahapadma Nanda was the dynasty's founder.

 

• The Nandas united a large area under Magadha, which was a major step toward the Mauryan empire. Kalinga is the clearest example in the notes of their conquests.

 

• Their reign ended with Dhananda, the ninth ruler.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Nandas conquered Kalinga before Ashoka.

 

• The ninth Nanda ruler closed the dynasty.

 

• Panini lived in their time.

 

• The Hathigumpha inscription is at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar in Odisha.

 

• Kharavela was king of Kalinga. Hathigumpha means 'elephant cave', and the inscription is dated to the 1st century BC. Other Nanda facts to remember: nine rulers, Mahapadma as the founder, Dhananda as last, and Panini in their time.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): R explains A, because the conquest of Kalinga was part of the extended Nanda empire. This choice wrongly says the reason does not explain the assertion.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): R is a true fact recorded in the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela. This choice wrongly calls the reason false even though the inscription records it.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): A is true, since the Nandas are regarded as the first empire builders of India. This choice wrongly calls the assertion false.

question:
Assertion (A): Chandragupta Maurya and Kautilya could launch a popular movement against the Nandas.

Reason (R): People deeply resented the harsh way the last Nanda ruler collected taxes.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Public anger over Dhananda's harsh tax collection gave Chandragupta and Kautilya the popular support to overthrow Nanda rule (धनानंद — कठोर कर, चंद्रगुप्त-कौटिल्य आंदोलन)

 

• The Nanda ruler targeted by the movement was the final king of the line.

 

• The movement led to the founding of the Mauryan Empire.

 

• Alexander's invasion occurred during this period.

 

• Public discontent made the overthrow of Dhananda easier for Chandragupta. Kautilya planned the movement and the Nandas were replaced by the Mauryas.

 

• The period also coincided with the invasion of Alexander in the north-west.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kautilya is also known as Chanakya.

 

• Chandragupta Maurya ruled from Pataliputra.

 

• The Nanda empire was rich but unpopular.

 

• Kautilya is the author of the Arthashastra.

 

• The Mauryan Empire was founded around 321 BC. Dhananda's wealth is said to have been so great that the Nandas became proverbial for riches in ancient tradition.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): R is the correct explanation of A, since the taxation anger gave the movement a mass base. This choice wrongly says the reason is not the explanation.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): R is true, as the notes say people deeply resented harsh tax collection. This choice wrongly calls the reason false, which contradicts the notes.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): A is true, since Chandragupta and Kautilya did launch a popular movement against the Nandas. This choice wrongly calls the assertion false.

question: Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the dynasties of Magadha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is Haryanka (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Udayin), then Shishunaga (Shishunaga, Kalasoka), then Nanda (Mahapadma Nanda to Dhananda) (हर्यंक → शिशुनाग → नंद)

 

• The Nandas were succeeded by the Mauryas under Chandragupta.

 

• Bimbisara founded the first dynasty.

 

• After the Nanda kings (the ninth being the last), Chandragupta Maurya came next.

 

• Remember the order by the founders: Bimbisara, Shishunaga, Mahapadma Nanda. After the Nandas came Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• Capital shifts in order: Rajagriha, Pataliputra, Vaishali, and then Pataliputra again. The order Haryanka-Shishunaga-Nanda also follows the shift in capitals. Rajagriha served the early Haryankas, Pataliputra was founded by Udayin, and Vaishali was used by Shishunaga. After the Nandas, the Mauryas made Pataliputra their imperial capital, which completes the political chain of early Magadha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Capitals: Rajagriha, Pataliputra, Vaishali, Pataliputra.

 

• The Nandas had nine rulers.

 

• This order is a regular SSC question.

 

• The first dynasty, the Haryankas, began with Bimbisara as per the notes.

 

• The Nandas had nine rulers in all. The Nanda rulers also had the support of a large army, which Greek writers noted.

 

NOTE

 

• Shishunaga, Haryanka, Nanda (Option 1): The Shishunagas came after the Haryankas, not before them. So the order beginning with the Shishunagas is wrong, since Bimbisara's dynasty was the first.

 

• Nanda, Haryanka, Shishunaga (Option 2): The Nandas were the last of the three dynasties and cannot come first. The order must begin with the Haryankas and end with the Nandas.

 

• Haryanka, Nanda, Shishunaga (Option 4): The Nandas came after the Shishunagas, not before them. The order cannot place the Nandas in the second position, because Mahapadma Nanda replaced the Shishunagas.

question: Which of the following Mahajanapada-capital pairs is NOT correctly matched?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Malla - Taxila.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Malla - Taxila is incorrect because the Malla capital was Kushinagar, while Taxila was the capital of Gandhara (मल्ल — कुशीनगर, तक्षशिला — गांधार)

 

• The other pairs are right: Avanti-Ujjain, Kuru-Indraprastha, Kashi-Varanasi.

 

• Kushinagar is where the Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana.

 

• Taxila was a famous centre of learning.

 

• Taxila belonged to Gandhara in the north-west, whereas the Malla capital was Kushinagar. This swap is a typical exam trap.

 

• Such 'not correctly matched' questions require you to know every capital with its state.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gandhara - Taxila; Vajji - Vaishali.

 

• Kosala - Sravasti; Vatsa - Kausambi.

 

• Magadha - Rajagriha.

 

• Kushinagar lies in eastern Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Kuru lay in the Delhi-Meerut region of the Ganga-Yamuna doab. Malla territory lay in the area of Kushinagar and Pava, and these towns are linked with the last days of both the Buddha and Mahavira.

 

NOTE

 

• Avanti - Ujjain (Option 1): Avanti-Ujjain is correctly paired. Ujjain was the capital of Avanti, so this is not the wrongly matched pair that the question asks for.

 

• Kuru - Indraprastha (Option 3): Kuru-Indraprastha is correctly paired. Indraprastha was the capital of Kuru, so this pair is right and cannot be the incorrect one asked for.

 

• Kashi - Varanasi (Option 4): Kashi-Varanasi is correctly paired. Varanasi was the capital of Kashi, hence this cannot be the pair that is incorrectly matched.

question: Which was the earliest capital of Magadha, before Pataliputra became the capital?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajagriha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rajagriha (Rajgir) was the capital of Magadha before Pataliputra, which was later founded by Udayin (राजगृह — मगध की प्रारंभिक राजधानी)

 

• The iron ores in the hills near Rajgir contributed to Magadha's strength.

 

• Pataliputra later became the imperial capital of the Mauryas.

 

• Shishunaga moved the capital to Vaishali.

 

• A PYQ asks 'Rajagriha was the capital of which Mahajanapada' and the answer is Magadha. Later the capital moved to Pataliputra.

 

• Bimbisara and Ajatashatru both ruled from Rajagriha. Rajagriha's natural defences came from the ring of hills around it, which also made it a secure capital for Bimbisara and Ajatashatru. The nearby hills also held iron ores, which fed the weapons industry of the early Magadhan state.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rajagriha was also called Girivraja.

 

• Bimbisara ruled from Rajagriha.

 

• The First Buddhist Council met near Rajgir.

 

• Rajagriha is modern Rajgir in Nalanda district of Bihar.

 

• The First Buddhist Council was held at Rajgir. Rajagriha is also known as Girivraja, meaning a hill-surrounded city, which fits its natural defences. Pataliputra, the next capital, was founded by Udayin and later served the Mauryas as the imperial capital.

 

NOTE

 

• Kausambi (Option 2): Kausambi was the capital of Vatsa, so it was not Magadha's earliest capital. The question is about Magadha, whose early capital lay in Bihar.

 

• Sravasti (Option 3): Sravasti was the capital of Kosala, not of Magadha. It lay in Uttar Pradesh and cannot be the early capital of Magadha.

 

• Champa (Option 4): Champa was the capital of Anga, which Magadha later absorbed. It was not itself a Magadhan capital, although it lay in the same region.

question: Which Haryanka king was a contemporary of both Mahavira and Buddha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bimbisara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bimbisara was a contemporary of both Mahavira and Buddha (बिंबिसार — महावीर और बुद्ध के समकालीन)

 

• He ruled Magadha in the 6th century BC from Rajagriha.

 

• His marriage alliances were with Kosala and Vaishali.

 

• He was killed by Ajatashatru.

 

• Mahavira and Buddha taught in Magadha and neighbouring areas under the patronage of kings. Bimbisara is the best-known royal contemporary.

 

• Bimbisara is said to have met the Buddha according to Buddhist tradition. The Veluvana grove at Rajagriha was donated to the Buddhist sangha by Bimbisara, showing his patronage. This patronage is one reason why the king is often connected with both the Buddha and Mahavira.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahavira and Buddha lived in the 6th-5th century BC.

 

• Magadha was the main centre of both religions.

 

• Ajatashatru also knew the Buddha.

 

• Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism.

 

• The Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya in Magadha. The Buddha spent several rainy seasons at Rajagriha during Bimbisara's reign, and the king gave the Veluvana grove to the sangha.

 

NOTE

 

• Udayin (Option 1): Udayin lived after Bimbisara and Ajatashatru. Only Bimbisara is linked in the notes with the lifetime of both Mahavira and Buddha.

 

• Kalasoka (Option 2): Kalasoka belonged to the Shishunaga dynasty and ruled about a century later. He was therefore not a contemporary of the two founders.

 

• Mahapadma Nanda (Option 3): Mahapadma Nanda lived in the 4th century BC, long after the two teachers. He is not the king referred to in the question.

question: Kakavarman, the successor of Shishunaga, is better known in history as:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kalasoka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kakavarman, the son and successor of Shishunaga, is also called Kalasoka; the Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali (383 BC) was held in his reign (काकवर्ण — कालाशोक)

 

• He belonged to the Shishunaga dynasty, which followed the Haryankas.

 

• Shishunaga had shifted the capital to Vaishali.

 

• The Shishunagas were followed by the Nandas.

 

• Kalasoka should not be confused with Ashoka, who was a Mauryan emperor. Kalasoka is the son of Shishunaga.

 

• His reign saw the Second Buddhist Council. Kakavarman and Kalasoka are two names for the same Shishunaga king, one from Puranic tradition and one from Buddhist chronicles. The notes give his dates by tying him to the Second Council at Vaishali in 383 BC.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalasoka should not be confused with the Mauryan Ashoka.

 

• The Second Council dealt with monastic discipline disputes.

 

• The Third Council was under Ashoka at Pataliputra.

 

• The Shishunaga dynasty followed the Haryankas.

 

• It ended when the Nandas took over. Kakavarman is the Puranic name of the king, whereas Buddhist texts call him Kalasoka.

 

NOTE

 

• Udayin (Option 2): Udayin was a Haryanka king, the son of Ajatashatru, who founded Pataliputra. He is not Kakavarman, who belonged to the later Shishunaga dynasty.

 

• Dhananda (Option 3): Dhananda belongs to the Nanda dynasty. He is not connected with Kakavarman, who was the Shishunaga ruler and son of Shishunaga.

 

• Ajatashatru (Option 4): Ajatashatru was a Haryanka king, the son of Bimbisara. Kakavarman belongs to the Shishunaga dynasty that came after the Haryankas.
